title: Baghdad to Córdoba: the Oud, the School, and a Civilization of Taste
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Baghdad, the Making of a Prodigy

stops.name: Baghdad, the house of the mawali of al-Mahdi
stops.campa: Ziryab is born in Baghdad into a family bound in clientage to the house of the Caliph al-Mahdi, in the city Mansur built round as the compass draws it, at the hinge of the Tigris trade. 'Ali ibn Nafi' is the name he is given; Ziryab, blackbird, is the name Baghdad gives him, for his dark skin and the carrying sweetness of his voice, and it is the one that outlasts him by a thousand years. The chroniclers disagree on nearly everything else, but agree that from childhood his ear set him apart, and that Baghdad was the only school large enough to hold him.
stops.quote: on account of his dark complexion, the clarity of his voice, and the sweetness of his character
stops.quote_source: Ibn Hayyan, on the origin of the epithet Ziryab (blackbird), preserved in al-Maqqari's Nafh al-Tib
suggested_refs: Abbasid Baghdad's Round City, the world capital where the caliphal court gathered its musicians
sources: Dwight Reynolds, 'Al-Maqqari's Ziryab: The Making of a Myth', Middle Eastern Literatures 11:2 (2008)

stops.name: Baghdad, apprenticed to Ishaq al-Mawsili
stops.campa: The boy is given into the house of Ishaq al-Mawsili, the reigning master of Baghdad's music and favourite of caliphs, in an age when a singer's throat could buy a palace. Ziryab studies the modes, the poetry, the etiquette of the majlis, and above all the discipline of the voice: how to hold breath, how to ornament a line without breaking it, how to enter and leave a song cleanly. He is the most gifted pupil in a house that has trained the gifted for two generations, and everyone who hears him rehearse says so openly.
suggested_refs: Kitab al-Aghani ('Book of Songs') of Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani, chronicling the Mawsili house of musicians
sources: Muslim Heritage, 'Ziryab: the Musician, Astronomer, Fashion Designer and Gastronome'

stops.name: Baghdad, before the Commander of the Faithful
stops.campa: Ishaq, proud of his pupil, brings Ziryab to sing before Harun al-Rashid himself. The young man takes up the oud and does something no one in the hall has heard: a fifth pair of strings sings out above the customary four, struck not with the usual wood but with the quill of an eagle's feather, bright and quick against the gut. The caliph, delighted, presses him with questions about a rare and difficult repertoire; Ziryab answers each one, note for note, verse for verse, until the hall itself seems to hold its breath, and Harun asks for him again.
suggested_refs: The five-course oud, its fifth string Ziryab's addition, standard in Arab lutherie ever since

stops.name: Baghdad, the master's jealousy
stops.campa: Favor has a price at court, and Ishaq watches his pupil's rise with a dread he cannot say aloud. He goes to the caliph before Ziryab can be summoned a third time and unmakes him with a single accusation: the young man is possessed, given to fits of frenzy horrible to witness, convinced the jinn speak to him in his sleep and hand him his songs. It works. The invitations stop. Ziryab, who has done nothing but sing what he heard, understands that Baghdad has no room left standing for two masters of the oud.
stops.quote: The young man is possessed. He's subject to fits of frenzy that are horrible to witness. He believes the jinn speak with him and inspire his music. He's so vain he believes his talent is unequaled in the world.
stops.quote_source: Ishaq al-Mawsili, as reported by Ibn Hayyan and rendered by Reinhart Dozy, Histoire des Musulmans d'Espagne
suggested_refs: Ibn Hayyan's Kitab al-Muqtabis, source of the jealousy narrative later expanded by al-Maqqari
sources: Reinhart Dozy, Histoire des Musulmans d'Espagne
History in the Margins, 'The Blackbird Sings'

stops.name: Baghdad, the exile's gift and the road out
stops.campa: Ishaq finishes what the accusation began, coming to Ziryab himself with money in hand: leave Baghdad, settle far from here, swear I will never hear your name again, and this will meet your needs. The city gives him reason enough besides; the throne has passed from Harun through the brothers' war between al-Amin and al-Ma'mun, and the capital that made him is no longer the capital he is leaving. Ziryab takes the purse, takes the oath, and turns west, carrying nothing of Baghdad but its music and a few remembered lines about a garden he will not see again.
stops.quote: Neither plump nor thin, neither tall nor short — what glorious days we had, spent at Dayr al-Matira; their only lack, for the lovelorn one, was that they were too few.
stops.quote_source: Verses attributed to Ziryab, preserved in al-Maqqari's Nafh al-Tib (cited in Reynolds, 'Al-Maqqari's Ziryab')
suggested_refs: Dayr al-Matira, the Baghdad-area monastery-garden of the verses' nostalgia, a favored excursion of Abbasid poets
sources: Dwight Reynolds, 'Al-Maqqari's Ziryab: The Making of a Myth'

stops.name: Damascus, the first refuge
stops.campa: The road out of Mesopotamia runs first to Damascus, old capital of the Umayyads whom Baghdad's own dynasty unseated two generations before, an irony Ziryab can hardly miss, riding as an Abbasid exile into a city that remembers the family he is about to serve on the far shore of the Mediterranean. He lingers only long enough to rest the animals and take the measure of the roads west, a singer without a court now, his Baghdad fame already turning into rumor that outpaces him on every caravan road.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad Mosque of Damascus, monument of the dynasty whose fortunes Ziryab's road will eventually rejoin in Córdoba

stops.name: Fustat, on the Nile
stops.campa: He crosses into Egypt and rests a season at Fustat on the Nile, the old garrison capital before Cairo existed, a caravan city thick with merchants and scholars moving between the Hejaz, Ifriqiya, and the Abbasid heartland. Word of the singer from Baghdad's court precedes him in the trading houses; he is asked to perform, and does, gathering along the way both a growing name and letters of introduction toward the Aghlabid court at Kairouan, where a ruler with money and ambition is known to want for a great musician of his own.
suggested_refs: Fustat, Egypt's Nile-side capital before Cairo, waystation of the ninth-century Mediterranean trade roads
sources: Muslim Heritage, 'Ziryab: the Musician, Astronomer, Fashion Designer and Gastronome'

stops.name: Kairouan, into the service of Ziyadat Allah
stops.campa: At Kairouan, the Aghlabid capital of Ifriqiya and holy city of the Maghreb, Ziryab enters the court of the emir Ziyadat Allah I, whose family has ruled since Baghdad delegated the province to keep it quiet and rich. The Great Mosque of Kairouan is rising anew under Aghlabid money; the court is proud, wealthy, and hungry for the polish of the Abbasid capital it can never quite equal. Ziryab, a genuine article out of Harun al-Rashid's own Baghdad, is exactly the ornament such a court craves, and Ziyadat Allah receives him with honor and a stipend.
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of Kairouan (Uqba Mosque), rebuilt and enlarged under the Aghlabids in these same years
sources: Mahmoud Guettat, 'Ziryab, Master of Andalusian Music', UNESCO Courier (1992)

stops.name: Kairouan, the years of favor
stops.campa: For a time the arrangement suits both men. Ziryab performs, teaches, composes; the Aghlabid court adopts something of the manners he brings from the caliphal capital, and his reputation, already large, grows larger across the western sea. But an emir's favor is a narrower shelter than a caliph's, and Ziryab has already once watched a great patron's warmth curdle overnight into suspicion. He does not yet know that Ifriqiya, too, is a way station and not a destination, only that the songs he composes here will travel further than he himself will.
suggested_refs: The Aghlabid court of Kairouan, ninth-century meeting point of Baghdad's music and the Maghreb

stops.name: Kairouan, the song that gives offense
stops.campa: A verse Ziryab sets to music, whether aimed carelessly or read too carefully, lands wrong in the emir's court; the chroniclers cannot agree what the offense was, only that it was taken as one. Ziyadat Allah, who a season before could not honor him enough, now condemns him to the lash and orders him out of Ifriqiya entirely. It is Baghdad and Ishaq again, the same shape of catastrophe in a different tongue: a gift too bright for the room it is given in, a patron who cannot bear to be outshone by his own ornament.
suggested_refs: The Aghlabid emirate's turbulent court politics, recorded in the later Ifriqiyan chronicles

stops.name: Kairouan, the road out to the strait
stops.campa: A second time Ziryab gathers what he owns — his wife, his sons, his daughters, his instruments — and puts a hostile court behind him, turning now north and west along the coast road toward the strait that divides Ifriqiya from Iberia. He carries a letter, sent ahead in hope rather than certainty, to al-Hakam I, the Umayyad emir of Córdoba, offering his service; the reply, when it finally comes, will find him already most of the way to the water, with nothing left to do but wait on a foreign shore.
suggested_refs: The Maghreb coast road linking Kairouan to the Strait of Gibraltar, the ninth-century route west

stops.name: Ceuta, the last African shore
stops.campa: At Sabta, Ceuta, the family stands at the narrowest gate of the Mediterranean, where Africa and Europe close to a strait a strong swimmer could almost cross. A ship is found, and Ziryab, his wife, his eight sons and two daughters, and whatever instruments and household goods have survived two exiles, are loaded aboard for the short, decisive crossing that Tariq ibn Ziyad's army made a century before him, though this invasion carries only an oud, a household, and a fading hope of employment on the far shore.
suggested_refs: The Strait of Gibraltar at its narrowest, the crossing point of Umayyad Iberia since Tariq ibn Ziyad
sources: Cherif Abderrahman Jah, 'A Musical Interlude', Critical Muslim

stops.name: Algeciras, the news of al-Hakam's death
stops.campa: The ship makes land at al-Jazira al-Khadra, Algeciras, the Umayyad emirate's own gate on the Iberian shore. Ziryab steps onto Andalusi ground to learn, within hours, that the emir who invited him, al-Hakam I, died in May, six weeks before the crossing; the letter he answered no longer has anyone alive to honor it. He and his household stand on the dock of a foreign country with no post, no patron, and a long sea behind them; the natural counsel is to turn back to Ifriqiya, and for a bitter day or two Ziryab very nearly takes it.
suggested_refs: The medieval port of Algeciras (al-Jazira al-Khadra), gateway of the Umayyad crossing from Africa

stops.name: Algeciras, the word of Abu al-Nasr Mansur
stops.campa: Word of the stranded Baghdadi musician reaches Abu al-Nasr Mansur, a Jewish singer high in the confidence of the Córdoban court, who has heard enough of Ziryab's name to recognize what has just washed up on the emirate's own shore. He writes at once to the new emir, al-Hakam's son Abd al-Rahman II, urging him not to let a talent of this order slip back across the strait for want of a renewed invitation. It is a stranger's word, offered without payment, that turns Ziryab's fortune a second time, toward, and not away from, a throne.
suggested_refs: Abu al-Nasr Mansur, the Jewish court musician whose recommendation reopened Ziryab's road to Córdoba

stops.name: Algeciras, the invitation renewed
stops.campa: The reply comes back from Córdoba in Abd al-Rahman II's own hand: the invitation his father made stands renewed, and more besides, a post at court, a household provided, a welcome that owes nothing now to al-Hakam's memory and everything to Abu al-Nasr Mansur's letter. Ziryab, who two days before was pricing passage back to Kairouan, orders the family's baggage turned around instead, inland, toward a city he has never seen and a young emir he has never met, on the strength of one stranger's good word.
suggested_refs: The letters exchanged between Algeciras and Córdoba that reopened Ziryab's invitation, 822

stops.name: Córdoba, the audience with Abd al-Rahman II
stops.campa: Ziryab is brought before Abd al-Rahman II, an emir near his own age, cultivated and curious, who has waited since his father's day for exactly this ornament to his court. The terms settled that day become famous in themselves: two hundred gold dinars a month, five hundred more at midsummer and at the new year, a thousand at each of the two great feasts, grain and barley by the measure, a house in the city, and productive farms in the countryside besides. No musician in the western world has ever been paid like this. Ziryab accepts, and Baghdad, at last, recedes behind him.
suggested_refs: The Alcázar of the Umayyad emirs at Córdoba, seat of the audience and Ziryab's patron court
sources: Dwight Reynolds, 'Abd al-Rahman II and Ziryab, 822-852'

stops.name: Córdoba, nadim to the emir
stops.campa: Beyond his salary Ziryab becomes something rarer still: the emir's nadim, his boon companion, present at table and in counsel, consulted on matters far outside music, geography, the stars, the calendar, the correct way to dress a wound or season a dish. Abd al-Rahman II, whose own court is eager to rival Baghdad's glamour without ever having seen it, treats Ziryab as a living transcript of the caliphal capital and defers to him accordingly. Within a few years the court of Córdoba begins to look less like a frontier emirate and more like Baghdad's own western mirror.
suggested_refs: The office of nadim (boon companion) at the Umayyad court, Ziryab's role beside Abd al-Rahman II
sources: Dwight Reynolds, 'Abd al-Rahman II and Ziryab, 822-852'

stops.name: Córdoba, the founding of the school
stops.campa: Ziryab founds a school of music in Córdoba open to noble and common pupils alike, an unheard-of mixing of rank that the court tolerates because the results are unarguable. His own household supplies half the enrollment — his eight sons and two daughters are raised inside the discipline from childhood — and around them gather the ambitious young of the whole city, taught not only songs but the theory beneath them: the modes, the poetic meters, the grammar of ornament. It is, by the account later ages give it, the first conservatory the world has seen.
stops.quote: the founder of the musical traditions of Islamic Spain
suggested_refs: The music school Ziryab founded at Córdoba, ancestor of the Andalusi conservatory tradition

stops.name: Córdoba, the discipline of the voice
stops.campa: His teaching is exacting to the point of severity. A pupil whose jaw will not open wide enough is made to hold a piece of wood between the back teeth until the mouth learns the shape a great voice requires. A sash is bound tight about the waist to force the breath to rise from the right place. He tests lung and will together by having students hold a single note as long as the body can sustain it, measuring them against his own memory of what Baghdad's masters once demanded of him. Ibn Hayyan will later set all of this down as fact, not exaggeration.
suggested_refs: Ibn Hayyan's Kitab al-Muqtabis, recording Ziryab's method of vocal training in detail

segments.name: The Fifth String and the Songs of the Jinn

stops.name: Córdoba, the oud remade
stops.campa: At Córdoba Ziryab completes the instrument he began remaking before Harun al-Rashid. The fifth pair of strings, first heard in Baghdad, is now given its full meaning: he dyes the oud's four old strings each a color standing for one of the humors of the body — black bile, yellow bile, blood, phlegm — and the new fifth string, set between them, he dyes red for the soul that governs all four. The eagle's quill replaces wood for good. Andalusi lutherie will follow this scheme for a thousand years without ever asking why.
suggested_refs: The five-course oud, its strings traditionally read as the four humors and the soul, per Ziryab's scheme
sources: Muslim Heritage, 'Ziryab: the Musician, Astronomer, Fashion Designer and Gastronome'

stops.name: Córdoba, the songs the jinn bring in sleep
stops.campa: Ziryab holds, and says openly, what Ishaq once used to ruin him: that in his sleep the jinn come and sing to him, whole melodies complete with their words, and that he wakes in the middle of the night unable to let the song go unrecorded. He rouses whichever students are near, teaches them the piece before the dream can fade, and returns to bed only once it is fixed. Ibn Hayyan records the practice without a flicker of doubt; in Córdoba, unlike Baghdad, no one dares call it madness.
suggested_refs: Ibn Hayyan's account of Ziryab's jinn-taught songs, later repeated by al-Maqqari in Nafh al-Tib
sources: History in the Margins, 'The Blackbird Sings'
Reinhart Dozy, Histoire des Musulmans d'Espagne

stops.name: Córdoba, the twenty-four nawbat
stops.campa: Out of his enormous store of melody Ziryab shapes twenty-four nawbat, one suite for each hour of the day, each built on its own mode, its own color, its own governing mood, a whole clock of music mapped onto the emotional life of a single revolution of the sun. It is the most ambitious act of composition the western Islamic world has yet seen, an architecture as much as a repertoire, and it will outlive every court that ever paid to hear it, surviving in fragments, under other names, into ages Ziryab cannot imagine.
suggested_refs: The nawba suite form, Ziryab's twenty-four-hour cycle, ancestor of Andalusi classical music's structure today
sources: Mahmoud Guettat, 'Ziryab, Master of Andalusian Music', UNESCO Courier

stops.name: Córdoba, a thousand songs remembered
stops.campa: By the account later chroniclers give, Ziryab's memory alone holds more than a thousand songs, each with its verses, its proper mode, and the occasion for which it was first made, a living library no library building of the age could have matched. Scholars centuries afterward will doubt whether one man's memory could truly hold so much, and will trace how each retelling of his life inflated the number further; but in Córdoba, where he sings from that memory nightly before the emir, no one doubts it, because they are hearing the proof themselves.
suggested_refs: The oral repertoire tradition Ziryab is credited with founding, carried memory to memory before any notation existed
sources: Dwight Reynolds, 'Al-Maqqari's Ziryab: The Making of a Myth'

stops.name: Córdoba, the calendar of clothes
stops.campa: Ziryab teaches Córdoba to dress by the season and even by the hour: bright colors and light fabrics in spring, white through the heat of summer, fur-trimmed and heavier cloth against winter, distinct dress again for morning audience and for the evening's wine and music. Nothing like it has organized Andalusi wardrobes before. The court adopts it first, then the merchants who supply the court, then, over generations, cities the emir will never visit; a fashion calendar invented for one man's taste quietly becomes the shape of how a civilization decides what to wear and when.
suggested_refs: The seasonal fashion calendar attributed to Ziryab, an early instance of dress organized by season and hour
sources: Cherif Abderrahman Jah, 'A Musical Interlude', Critical Muslim

stops.name: Córdoba, the new fashion of the hair
stops.campa: He remakes how Córdoba wears its hair and its face besides: a short, banged style that leaves the neck, the ears, and the eyebrows bare, replacing the long, ear-covering braids women have worn for generations; close shaving for the men who follow the court's lead; new depilatory pastes, shaped eyebrows, scented oils worked through the hair in place of plain rosewater. What begins as the emir's own household style spreads outward through the merchant class, then further, until Córdoba's streets themselves look visibly different from what they looked like a decade before.
suggested_refs: The short banged hairstyle attributed to Ziryab, replacing the long ear-covering braids of earlier Andalusi fashion
sources: Cherif Abderrahman Jah, 'A Musical Interlude', Critical Muslim

stops.name: Córdoba, tooth-powder and the morning bath
stops.campa: Among the smaller reforms that outlast him: a dentifrice of his own recipe, described as both effective and pleasant to the taste, and a preparation against the odor of the body, urged on the court alongside a discipline of washing morning and evening that many Córdobans have not troubled with before. It is easy, from a great distance, to laugh at hygiene as a legacy; it is harder to find another single figure credited with moving an entire city's daily habit of the body, and Andalusi writers a century later still trace the custom back to him by name.
suggested_refs: An early dentifrice recipe attributed to Ziryab, among the first recorded in the western Islamic world
sources: premierepeau.com, 'Ziryab: The Man Who Invented Seasonal Fragrance, Deodorant, and the Three-Course Meal'

stops.name: Córdoba, the table remade
stops.campa: At the emir's table Ziryab replaces the old custom of setting everything out on one broad platter with a sequence of his own design: soup first, then meat or fowl or fish, then fruit and sweets and nuts to close the meal, each course cleared before the next arrives, all of it laid on fine leather rather than bare wood. He is credited too with putting asparagus on Andalusi tables for the first time, and with replacing the court's heavy metal drinking vessels with crystal, so the wine, or in devout households the sherbet, can be seen as well as tasted.
suggested_refs: The three-course meal — soup, main course, dessert — attributed to Ziryab's reform of Córdoba's table service

stops.name: Córdoba, chess, polo, and the astrologers from India
stops.campa: Ziryab's curiosity runs well past music and manners. He brings word and practice of games newly fashionable at Baghdad — chess foremost among them, and a form of polo — into the Córdoban court's leisure, and is said to have encouraged the arrival of astrologers out of India, carrying methods of reading the stars the Umayyad court had not seen before. Little of this survives as clearly attributed fact the way the oud or the nawbat do, but the pattern holds: whatever the wider Abbasid world knows, Córdoba, through Ziryab, comes to know shortly after.
suggested_refs: Chess, carried west into Umayyad Córdoba's court leisure in Ziryab's generation
sources: Cherif Abderrahman Jah, 'A Musical Interlude', Critical Muslim

stops.name: Córdoba, the Mezquita rising alongside him
stops.campa: Through these same years Abd al-Rahman II enlarges the Great Mosque of Córdoba, extending Abd al-Rahman I's original hall further south with new bays of the same red-and-white striped arches, a building program running in parallel with everything Ziryab is doing to the emirate's taste in music, dress, and food. Patron and nadim are remaking Córdoba together, one in stone and one in habit, and the city that results — mosque, table, wardrobe, and song reorganized within a single generation — will be remembered as the moment Córdoba stopped imitating Baghdad and became a capital in its own right.
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of Córdoba (Mezquita), enlarged under Abd al-Rahman II during Ziryab's years at court

stops.name: Córdoba, the taste that outran the court
stops.campa: What begins inside the palace does not stay there. Merchants who supply the emir's household adopt his fashions to sell them; the upper classes of the city copy the court that copies Ziryab; and in time, so the Andalusi chroniclers claim, something of it passes even to Córdoba's Christian and Jewish neighbors, and outward again along the trade roads into the rest of Europe, the seasonal wardrobe, the ordered courses of a formal meal, the crystal glass, habits so thoroughly absorbed within a few centuries that no one drinking from a stemmed glass in Paris or Toledo will remember where the custom started.
suggested_refs: The spread of Ziryab's court customs beyond Córdoba into the wider Iberian and European world, per later Andalusi chroniclers
sources: Cherif Abderrahman Jah, 'A Musical Interlude', Critical Muslim

segments.name: The House of Nafi': Elder Years and Death

stops.name: Córdoba, the house of eight sons and two daughters
stops.campa: Ziryab's own household becomes, in effect, the second generation of his school. His son Ubayd Allah grows into the most celebrated singer of the family after his father; his daughter Hamduna, trained alongside her brothers, marries into the vizierate; another daughter, Ulaiya, absorbs more of his personal repertoire and his surviving students than any of her siblings. Five of the eight sons and both daughters build careers as musicians in their own right, so that by Ziryab's later years half the notable voices of Córdoba trace their training to one house on one street.
suggested_refs: The musical dynasty of Ziryab's children, who inherited and extended the Córdoba school after him
sources: Cherif Abderrahman Jah, 'A Musical Interlude', Critical Muslim

stops.name: Córdoba, thirty years the emir's companion
stops.campa: Nearly three decades on from the audience that made him nadim, Ziryab is still at Abd al-Rahman II's side, an old man now by the standards of the age, his hair gone from the black of a Baghdad prodigy to the grey of a Córdoban institution. The arrangement between them, once a gamble on a stranded refugee, has become the single fact every visiting embassy is told about the Umayyad court: that its emir keeps at his table the greatest musician the western world has produced, and pays him like it.
suggested_refs: Thirty years of patronage between Abd al-Rahman II and Ziryab, 822-852, the longest such partnership in Umayyad Córdoba
sources: Dwight Reynolds, 'Abd al-Rahman II and Ziryab, 822-852'

stops.name: Córdoba, the death of the emir
stops.campa: Abd al-Rahman II dies in the year 852, after thirty years on the Córdoban throne, and the court Ziryab did so much to shape passes to his son Muhammad I. The new emir has grown up inside the world Ziryab built — the music, the table, the dress — and continues the patronage more or less unbroken, but something of the original partnership, the two men near in age who remade a capital together, cannot be renewed with a different sovereign. Ziryab, past sixty now, keeps his school, his salary, and his household, and outlives his great patron by five years.
suggested_refs: Muhammad I of Córdoba, Abd al-Rahman II's son and successor, who inherited Ziryab's patronage

stops.name: Córdoba, the death of Ziryab
stops.campa: Ziryab dies in Córdoba in the year 857, in the city he reached as a penniless exile thirty-five years before and leaves as the founder of its music, its table, and half its manners. Al-Maqqari, writing centuries afterward but drawing on the Córdoban record, sums up what the whole tradition agrees on beneath its disagreements over dates and anecdotes: that there was never, before him or after him, a man of his profession more generally beloved and admired. He is buried in the city that paid him like a prince for the privilege of being remade by him.
stops.quote: There never was, either before or after him, a man of his profession who was more generally beloved and admired.
suggested_refs: Al-Maqqari's Nafh al-Tib, the seventeenth-century compilation preserving the fullest account of Ziryab's life and death

stops.name: Tétouan, the Kunnash al-Ha'ik gathers what remains
stops.campa: Nine and a half centuries after Ziryab shapes his twenty-four nawbat, one for each hour, the Moroccan poet and musician Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Ha'ik sits in Tétouan and gathers into a single songbook, the Kunnash, whatever of that vast structure still survives in living memory: eleven nawbat of the original twenty-four, their poems and their modal architecture fixed at last in writing after a thousand years of mouth-to-ear transmission. What Ziryab began as a courtier's private repertoire in Córdoba becomes, through al-Ha'ik's book, the fixed canon still performed today by the Andalusi orchestras of Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Libya, the blackbird's furthest and longest-carrying song.
suggested_refs: The Kunnash al-Ha'ik (Tétouan, c. 1785), the songbook preserving eleven of Ziryab's twenty-four nawbat, still played by Andalusi orchestras across the Maghreb today
sources: Afropop Worldwide, interview with Dwight Reynolds, 'Al-Andalus 2: North Africa and Beyond'
